Portfolio risk study · Python, SQL · data to 2026-10-14

Does rebalancing make a BTC/ETH portfolio safer?

This study tests whether rebalancing, or weighting by volatility, reduces the drawdowns of a two-asset BTC/ETH portfolio compared with buying and holding, and what it costs in return and trading. Rules were tuned on 2016-11 to 2021-12 and then judged once on 2022-01 to 2026-10.

Buy & hold 50/50, max drawdown-69%
Best pure rebalancing rule-68%
Volatility target, drawdown-picked-54%
90-day correlation, test median0.87

Findings

  1. Rebalancing between BTC and ETH did not reduce drawdowns. Out of sample, buy-and-hold 50/50 fell 69% from peak to trough. The calendar, threshold and inverse-volatility rules all fell between 68% and 69%, within about one percentage point of it. The two assets fell together: on days BTC dropped 5% or more, ETH also fell 98% of the time, and fell further on average (-8.6% vs -7.3%).
  2. Weighting by volatility mostly meant holding more BTC. ETH was the more volatile asset almost throughout, so minimum variance held about 89% BTC on average. Its 67% drawdown is about the same as holding only BTC (67%). It beat buy-and-hold (8.6% vs 4.1% CAGR) because BTC beat ETH in this period, not because it diversified better.
  3. Only holding cash cut drawdowns materially, and how the parameters were picked decided whether it did. Picked for the shallowest training drawdown, volatility targeting (a 40% target, 90-day lookback, monthly rebalancing) fell 54%, against 69% for buy-and-hold, holding 26% cash on average. Picked for the best training Calmar ratio, the same rule chose an 80% target. Volatility after 2022 rarely exceeded that target, so the rule held almost no cash (0.5%) and fell 70%, like buy-and-hold. The training period rewarded staying fully invested, because 2017 and 2020–21 were huge rallies.
  4. The drawdown reduction from holding cash is robust; the return gain is not. In 500 block-bootstrapped versions of the test period, the drawdown-picked volatility target had a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold in 97% of paths (median 10 points shallower). It had a higher CAGR in only 48% of them, so its 9.2% vs 4.1% CAGR in the actual test period was partly luck of timing. Over the longer walk-forward test from 2019, where parameters were re-picked each January, it fell 54% vs 77%, but returned 34% a year against 47%. That is the trade-off: shallower falls, smaller rallies. Quarterly 50/50 rebalancing had a shallower drawdown in only 27% of bootstrap paths.
  5. Parameter rankings did not carry over from training to testing. For volatility targeting, the Spearman rank correlation of Calmar between training and test was -0.87, so the order almost reversed. For inverse volatility it was -0.02. Fine-tuning lookbacks and rebalancing frequencies mostly fits noise. The choice of rule matters far more than its settings.
  6. Trading costs were small next to these effects. The 50/50 rebalancing rules traded 0.1–0.8× the portfolio a year, costing at most 0.19% a year at 25 bps. They trailed buy-and-hold even when trading was free. Minimum variance and the drawdown-picked volatility target stayed ahead of buy-and-hold up to about 238 and 451 bps per unit traded. Trading at the signal's own close instead of the next day's changed CAGR by at most 0.5 points and max drawdown by at most 0.9 points.

Block bootstrap of the test period

Each of the 500 paths resamples the test period's joint BTC/ETH daily returns in blocks averaging 30 days. This keeps crashes and their co-movement intact. Every signal is then rebuilt from the resampled path. The bootstrap tests whether a result depends on the order of events. It cannot test a change of regime, because every path reuses the test period's own returns.

Method

  • Question. Do rebalancing and volatility-based weighting reduce a BTC/ETH portfolio's drawdowns compared with buy-and-hold, and what do they give up in return and turnover?
  • Data. Daily USD candles (00:00 UTC close) from Coinbase Exchange, 2016-05-18 → 2026-10-14. Two missing ETH days in May 2016, inside the warm-up period, carry the previous close forward. The Coinbase closes were cross-checked against Bitstamp: the daily-return correlation was 0.996 or higher, and the average absolute price gap was 0.12% or less. The largest gaps were in the December 2017 peak.
  • SQL layer. SQLite builds the gap-filled calendar, the returns, the rolling 30/60/90/180-day volatility and correlation (window aggregates), the drawdowns and the summary queries. A test checks the SQL statistics against pandas to 1e-10.
  • Rules. Buy-and-hold 50/50 (weights drift); calendar rebalancing to 50/50 (daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly); threshold rebalancing when BTC's weight drifts beyond a band (2.5–20%); inverse volatility; two-asset minimum variance (clipped to 0–100%); and a 50/50 volatility target that moves into cash when forecast volatility is above target (no leverage, cash earns 0%). In total 51 candidates across 5 families.
  • No look-ahead. Signals at close t use data up to close t, and trades fill at close t+1. A test changes the future returns and checks that no earlier result moves; the check also catches a rule that deliberately peeks ahead.
  • Out-of-sample. 180-day warm-up, then training 2016-11-15 → 2021-12-31 and testing 2022-01-01 → 2026-10-14. Parameters were chosen on training data only, then run once on the test period.
  • Costs and turnover. Turnover is the sum of |Δweight| across BTC and ETH, so swapping 10% of the portfolio from ETH to BTC counts as 0.2. The cost is that turnover times the bps rate. The opening allocation is free for every rule.
  • Annualisation. 365 days a year. Sharpe uses a 0% risk-free rate.

This is historical research on two assets over one decade, not investment advice. Ten years of crypto includes only about three full boom-and-bust cycles, so every conclusion here rests on a small number of crashes.
